content: Stephen Wolfram talked a lot about computational irreducibility. Does anyone have an idea on how we can formalize this notion?

An idea would be to attach a cost to each step of a computation. Then for many steps computation you have a cost that is the sum of each individual steps.
If there exists a function that reach the same computation with a lower cost than that, the computation would be reducible else it's irreducible.
Now proving that there exist no function that lowers the total cost would be an open problem. I don't think we have the tools to do so. Like today we have no clue how to prove that P != NP .

@Alfredo Moreira-Rosa I think we can start with some basic instances of CI we are already familiar, like the 3-body problem or Conway's Game of Life. Basically, what we can't have in both cases are formulas that allows us to predict the future state of these systems without just repeatedly applying their underlying rules

I think the notion of "computational irreducibility" is necessarily rather informal. And besides, saying that we can't do better "than just repeatedly applying their underlying rules" is ... not really true.

Conway's GoL does, for instance, benefit greatly from hashlife type acceleration. Empirically on random states it gives a big speedup, but it actually does so on highly structured instances too. For instance, if you build a Turing machine in GoL in the "standard" way, then hashlife gets you at least a quadratic acceleration (because large portions of the tape aren't changing step to step).

The 3-body-problem, too, is amenable to procedures like perturbation theory and Poincare maps, and these are used to great effect in astronomy to compute good predictions out to millions of years of planetary orbits.

Even the most generic "just evolve" problem would be something like: here's a black-box "f" from n bits to n bits. (For instance, SHA512 or something). What is the value of f applied k times to a given input? You can evaluate this in k steps, and that seems to be mostly the best you can do.

But once k exceeds 2^n, you can do better: run f for 2^n steps, at which point you will definitely have seen a cycle. (This only needs a constant factor extra space because of tortoise-hare algorithms.) Now for the remaining (k-2^n) steps, take it modulo the length of the cycle, and just skip ahead to that. This means you never need more than 2*2^n steps, so this is very far from computational irreducibility for k = 2^(2^n) -- even though we literally no nothing at all about the step and this applies to any time evolution procedure at all.

If someone required me to give the best formal definition I could, it would be something like:

Call a "computational process" a function from an initial state S0 and a monoid T to a current state S(T). T would usually be either natural numbers (for discrete steps) or the nonnegative reals, but you could also imagine T being a monoid of strings for instance (you're feeding an input strings into a transducer).

A "partially observable computational process" also carries a map o : S -> O, showing some partial observations of the state. We can talk about the set o⁻¹(o(S(T)), the set of all states that get mapped to the same observation.

Then you could call two partially observable computational processes equivalent if there are some mappings from each to emulate the other. These mappings can change the value of T, but I would say that it should be a constant factor that doesn't depend on the initial state. The mappings themselves should be 'nice' in some way I don't know how to pin down.
This is essentially saying that computational irreducibility is something like DTIME(n)-complete problems under sublinear time reductions.
... anyway, fun diversion that, but since "computational irreducibility" is very far from being an established or even precisely-defined term in literature, I don't think it makes sense to formalize.

Alex Meiburg said:

... anyway, fun diversion that, but since "computational irreducibility" is very far from being an established or even precisely-defined term in literature, I don't think it makes sense to formalize.

Well, I know that already. I just wanted to see if we can brainstorm some broad notions of what CI could be...

The formalization of computational irreducibility is the type classification of the observation process's Radon-Nikodym cocycle: a process is irreducible iff its conservative ergodic core has positive entropy rate and trivial acceleration group, and the admissible speedups are exactly the period group of the flow of weights, trivial for II₁, quantized by λ for III_λ, continuous for III₁. The "nice mappings" are Kakutani time-changes; the lower bound is Shannon-McMillan-Breiman via Kraft, with Abramov giving the exact exchange rate between time and entropy; cycle-skipping and hashlife are the Hopf-dissipative part and the zero-entropy factors, which is where all reducibility lives.

I initially thought exactly the same thing, computational irreducibility seemed to mean that, for some processes, there is simply no way to obtain the future state substantially faster than executing the underlying evolution.

Yet, working on a production reasoning graph protocol changed my perspective somehow. I now think there are 2 very different sources of computational cost that tend to be conflated.

One is the cost of evolving the process. The other is the cost of identifying the structurally relevant part of the state space.

If an instance can be decomposed structurally before the main search begins, the algorithm may avoid reasoning over the raw combinatorial space entirely. During inference, many configurations can be grouped because they have the same relevant continuation, the same constraints, the same interface behaviour, or the same consequences for the objective.

A generalized Sudoku is a simple example. The raw space of partial assignments is exponential, but propagation, symmetries, separators and identical residual candidate profiles can collapse large families of assignments into a much smaller set of structurally distinct states. Likewise, a single exact structural filter can eliminate an exponentially large family of candidates without inspecting them individually.

So I am no longer convinced that computational irreducibility should primarily mean that every intermediate step must be simulated. The more interesting question may be how much computational difficulty remains after all available exact structural decomposition and compression have been applied.

Hashlife and cycle-skipping then look like particular instances of a more general phenomenon... detect structure, identify equivalent future behaviour, compress the state space, and compute on the compressed representation.

From this perspective, irreducibility would concern the residual complexity that survives exact structural compression. The hard part is not showing that a particular acceleration fails, but showing that no further useful exact structural reduction exists.

@Daniel Sautot how could we formalize these 2 sources of computational cost as 2 quantities then?
Also, I think that the "original" notion of CI can be thought of as how much we can reduce the computatational cost after applying all these shortcuts

Honestly, based on the results I got, I think the structural cost can be formalized quite naturally, but I’m much less convinced that the residual cost after all possible shortcuts can be defined absolutely.

The structural cost can be quantified. It is the cost of extracting the relevant structure, constructing the decomposition, identifying equivalence classes, and compressing the state space before or during inference.

But the remaining cost after all "shortcuts" is different. All shortcuts is not a closed set. During inference, new exact filters can arise from very specific constraints, contradictions, bounds, symmetries, or combinations of properties of the current residual state. A single such filter may eliminate an exponentially large family of candidates without examining them individually.

There is therefore no reason to expect a finite or canonical enumeration of all possible exact filters. Their applicability may be arbitrarily specific to an instance or to a structural subclass. In my heuristic experiments, this is exactly what keeps happening, as the residual instance evolves, I repeatedly find new constraint interactions or contradictions that were not useful, or sometimes not even visible, at the initial stage.

So I think we can define residual complexity relative to a fixed class of admissible reductions, but not an absolute residual complexity after every possible structural shortcut. The latter would require establishing that no further exploitable exact structure exists.

This is why I would separate the two quantities. Structural decomposition and structural compression can be measured. Absolute computational irreducibility would require an exhaustiveness result over all possible exact structural reductions, which is, IMHO, a much stronger statement.
